solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Louche gents are ranked like Wilson, say

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase describing a rank stands for the noun naming that rank, the title Wilson held

indicators.note: louche means disreputable or shifty, so the letters behave badly and fall out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written, eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Some shady gentlemen are given a military rank like a character from an old sitcom.
explanation.walkthrough: Sergeant Wilson is the languid, gentlemanly sergeant in Dad's Army, a long-running British TV comedy about the wartime Home Guard; 'say' marks him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilson is a fictional holder of this non-commissioned army rank, so being ranked like him means holding that rank.

clue.text: This projects and protects borders of Sarawak, for example

indicators.note: the borders of a region are its edges, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the Malaysian state
the usual abbreviation, from Latin exempli gratia

explanation.surface: Something sticks out to guard the frontier of a Borneo state.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a riddle-like description: a skeg is the projecting after-part of a keel, which sticks out and shields the rudder.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat's keel extension both juts out below the hull and guards the rudder, matching the two verbs in the description.

clue.text: Happily see unit as part of a set (7, two words)

indicators.note: happily can mean by chance or haphazardly, so the letters fall together in a random order

blocks.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully views a unit belonging to a matching set, like flat-pack furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration '(7, two words)' tells you the seven letters split into a two-word French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase literally means in a sequence, forming one set with other things, as rooms or furniture can.

clue.text: Having switched Pirellis in Reno scrap register of reserves

blocks.note: Pirelli makes tyres, spelt tires in America (Reno is in Nevada), so a car given new ones has been re-tired
a scrap is a fight, and the lists were the arena for a joust, a list being a combat there

explanation.surface: A motorist in Nevada changes the tyres and junks the old set.
explanation.walkthrough: The first chunk is a pun: RE-TIRED, with the American spelling of tyre that 'in Reno' licenses. The retired list records officers who have left active service but may be recalled.
explanation.definitionFit: Military services keep a roll of retired officers, who form a reserve that can be called back in an emergency.

clue.text: Von der Leyen’s lot falls short so comes out

blocks.note: Ursula von der Leyen presides over the European Commission, abbreviated EC
to fall short in a contest is to be beaten

explanation.surface: The European Commission underachieves and so leaks or confesses something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comes out' is meant in the entomological sense: an insect ecloses when it emerges from the pupa or egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclosion is the emergence of an insect from its pupal case or egg, so this verb means it hatches or emerges.

clue.text: What grows in Spenser? A stanza, loosely Latin

blocks.note: taken as written
a strophe is a section of an ode, only loosely the same as a stanza, as the clue admits
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A reader asks what features in Spenser's poetry, answering with a free Latin verse form.
explanation.walkthrough: Spenser's elegy of this title names a plant (a starwort) that sprang up where the lovers died; Chambers keeps it as a Spenserian plant name.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser uses the word as the name of a flowering plant, a starwort, so it is literally something growing in his verse.

clue.text: One’s own old bustle

blocks.note: British slang: on one's tod means on one's own, from rhyming slang Tod Sloan
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone owns an antique bustle, the padded frame worn under Victorian skirts.
explanation.walkthrough: Tod Sloan was an American jockey whose name became rhyming slang for 'alone', so 'on your tod' means by yourself. 'Bustle' is not the dress frame but a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuss or commotion, all noise and activity, is a bustle in the sense of busy, excited movement.

clue.text: Cheers gripping Number One at first — there is no alternative

indicators.note: to grip something is to hold it tight, so one piece closes round the other
this places one piece ahead of the other in the inner pair

blocks.note: ta is British informal thanks
the Roman numeral
the abbreviation used in mathematics for a number

explanation.surface: A toast to the top person, followed by the claim that nobody else will do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number One' looks like a single unit, but it splits: Number gives N and One gives I, placed first. Read across with 1-across, the grid shows SERGEANT TINA, a nod to Margaret Thatcher's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The acronym was Margaret Thatcher's slogan for her economic policies and became her nickname.

clue.text: Fashion a line in keeping with key

blocks.note: le bon ton is high fashion, and ton alone means the prevailing mode
taken as written
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A designer creates a clothing line that suits an important look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion' looks like a verb meaning make; it is a noun giving the old word for the fashionable mode.
explanation.definitionFit: Music that keeps to a key centre is described this way, as opposed to atonal music which avoids one.

clue.text: Resort’s name is in the language of Horace

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation

blocks.clueFragment: is in the language of Horace
blocks.note: Horace wrote in Latin, where est is the word for 'is'

explanation.surface: A holiday resort's name turns out to be Latin, the language of a Roman poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort’s' reads as a possessive but stands for 'Resort is'. The resort is a haunt, not a seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: A haunt or snug retreat where someone habitually goes is a resort in the older sense, like a den or lair.

clue.text: Old language behind younger Fleming, say

blocks.note: American slang for the backside
a dictionary abbreviation for younger
Ian Fleming, creator of James Bond, is one bearer of the forename

explanation.surface: An old tongue spoken after a Flemish speaker, or by a junior Fleming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleming' tempts you toward Flemish or the Belgian language; the 'say' shows it is an example of a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Semitic tongue of Assyria, a dialect of Akkadian, is long extinct, making it an old language.

clue.text: Cleric may compromise this threnody delaying central part

definitions.note: a descriptive clause stands for the noun it describes, the joint a cleric bends

indicators.note: to delay something is to make it come later, so the middle letters arrive at the end instead

blocks.note: a keen is an Irish lament for the dead, a threnody

explanation.surface: A clergyman might weaken a funeral lament by holding back its middle section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Compromise' here means bend or put at risk: a cleric genuflecting bends the knee. The middle EE of the lament moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Genuflecting or kneeling in prayer bends the leg joint, so a priest is often putting strain on it.

clue.text: Society poets cavalierly gathering round vessels in dramas

indicators.note: acting cavalierly is acting offhandedly, without care, so the letters get careless treatment
to gather something is to take it in, so one piece is collected inside

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
taken as written, to be rearranged
a round letter

explanation.surface: Society poets carelessly gather around drinking cups described in plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled poets surround the O: TO(O)PES. 'Stoope' is the Shakespearean spelling of stoup, a drinking vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoups are drinking flagons; the old spelling appears in Elizabethan plays such as Hamlet, hence vessels in dramas.

clue.text: Catholic in free dailies and pro magazines and the like

indicators.note: something set free is loose and unconstrained, so the letters are released into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Catholic appears in free newspapers and professional magazines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' just places the C among the other letters before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Magazines, journals and newspapers are publications issued at regular intervals, so they form this class.

clue.text: With dense lists in renewal Debrett finally admitted formality

indicators.note: a renewal remakes something afresh, so the letters are put together anew
finally points at the end, so only the last letter is kept
to be admitted is to be let in, so one letter goes among the others

blocks.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange
the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A revised edition of Debrett's, the British guide to peerage and etiquette, is packed with lists and very formal.
explanation.walkthrough: Debrett's publishes the British peerage and etiquette guides, which fits the stiff surface; only its last letter joins the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff, unnatural formality in manner or writing is described as stilted, from walking on stilts.

clue.text: Instrument’s payment that helps around university

indicators.note: one piece sits around the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: a giro is a British state benefit payment, once paid by giro cheque
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A musical instrument is paid for with a student grant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instrument’s' means 'instrument is'. A giro in Britain was the cheque for welfare benefit, the payment that helps.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin American percussion instrument is a notched gourd scraped with a stick.

clue.text: Youngster, one will perhaps decline time of study

blocks.note: a pup is a cheeky young person
the Roman numeral
the contraction 'll, as in I'll
growing old is one kind of decline, hence 'perhaps'

explanation.surface: A pupil who might decline Latin nouns describes a period of learning.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nudges you to read 'Youngster, one will perhaps decline' as a pupil declining nouns; instead it splits into four small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The period of being a student, and in the law the year a trainee barrister spends as a pupil, is this.

clue.text: I come from north Africa, I’ll be cuddled by junior daughter

definitions.note: the setter writes in the first person as the animal, so 'I' stands for the noun

indicators.note: something cuddled is held in an embrace, so it sits inside

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation, as after a name
only the first letter, the pronoun, is kept; the contracted 'will' just carries the surface
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A North African speaks of being hugged by a little girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The jird is a gerbil of North Africa, and the clue is spoken in its voice, as a cuddly pet.
explanation.definitionFit: This desert rodent is a gerbil native to North Africa, so it could say it comes from there.

clue.text: Working arrangement from bawd belonging to patient chap?

blocks.note: the biblical Job is proverbial for patience, and 'belonging to' him makes the possessive form
bawd is an old word for a hare, punned on by Mercutio in Romeo and Juliet

explanation.surface: A deal struck with a brothel keeper owned by a long-suffering man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bawd' looks like a madam; it is the archaic hare. 'Belonging to' reverses the order so the patient man's possessive comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Two part-time workers splitting one full-time post is a standard employment arrangement.

clue.text: Isolated example of press being in fixed rut

indicators.note: something fixed has been adjusted or doctored, so the letters are rearranged
being inside something means sitting within it

blocks.note: o' is a shortened of, as in o'clock
to lie on something is to weigh or press on it
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lone case of the media stuck in a rut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like a link word joining definition to wordplay, but it supplies the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A data point or item far from the rest of a set is a statistical term for an isolated case.

clue.text: Sausage’s zing with a vegetable on being chopped

indicators.note: chopping cuts something off, so letters are removed

blocks.note: zing and pep both mean liveliness
as in 'ten pounds a day', a means per
a common vegetable
taken as written, the letters cut away

explanation.surface: A spicy sausage paired with chopped vegetables, like a pizza topping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being chopped' looks like kitchen prep, but it removes 'on' from the vegetable. 'Sausage’s' means 'Sausage is'.
explanation.definitionFit: This spicy Italian-American cured salami is a sausage, best known sliced on pizza.

clue.text: Nut to nibble nearly in its normal place

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: in printing, an en is called a nut, from the en-quad
taken as written
to pick at food is to nibble it

explanation.surface: A nut to snack on, almost where it should be.
explanation.walkthrough: Printers call an en space a nut, to tell it apart aloud from an em, called a mutton.
explanation.definitionFit: A medical term for an organ situated in its proper anatomical position, the opposite of ectopic.

clue.text: One put up rich source for master in Greek department

indicators.note: one thing given for another is a swap, so the first piece replaces the second

blocks.note: a nome was a province of ancient Greece or Egypt
a mine is a rich source, as in a mine of information
the abbreviation, as in MA, Master of Arts

explanation.surface: Someone proposed a wealthy backer in place of a master in a Greek faculty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek department' sounds like a university faculty; it is an administrative region. Swap its M for the rich source.
explanation.definitionFit: A candidate formally proposed for an office or award has been put up, in the sense of nominated.

clue.text: Dropping bribe in present

definitions.note: dropping is meant as spattering with drops, as rain bedashes

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: being means present or existing
in West Africa a dash is a tip or bribe

explanation.surface: Someone dropping a bribe into a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' is not a gift but the adjective for existing. To bedash is to bespatter, as rain does.
explanation.definitionFit: To bedash is to splash with drops, like rain, so the participle matches dropping in that sense.

clue.text: Sailor’s list containing alternate rope’s end that’s discarded

definitions.note: 'that's discarded' marks the term as obsolete

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: seel is a nautical word for a sudden heel or roll of a ship
the usual abbreviation

explanation.surface: A sailor's inventory includes a spare rope end that has been thrown away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor’s list' looks like a seaman's roster; it is the ship's lurch. The answer once meant a rope's end used to flog someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers records the phrase as an obsolete word for a rope's end used as a whip, so it is a discarded term.

clue.text: Most of crew will accept scan revealing roofs of a specific sort

indicators.note: most means not all, so the last letter is cut
accepting something takes it in, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a crew is a team
a CT scan, computed tomography

explanation.surface: Most of a work crew will agree to a scan showing particular kinds of roof.
explanation.walkthrough: These are anatomical roofs, as in the tectum of the midbrain, hence 'of a specific sort'.
explanation.definitionFit: In anatomy a roof-like structure such as part of the midbrain is a tectum, Latin for roof; this is its plural.

clue.text: Draw maiden in cascade’s pool

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: a lin or linn is a waterfall or the pool beneath it
the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: An artist sketches a young woman bathing in a waterfall's pool.
explanation.walkthrough: Lin, also spelt linn, is a Scots word for a waterfall or its plunge pool.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict or portray, especially in painting or outline, is an old verb for drawing.

clue.text: Cut down on additional premium

blocks.note: re means on or concerning
AP is the insurance abbreviation for additional premium

explanation.surface: An insurer cuts back on an extra charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut down' looks like reduce, but it is the harvesting sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Harvesting a crop with a scythe or sickle means mowing the stalks low, as farmers do at harvest.

clue.text: Crack mnemonic not socially agreeable

indicators.note: not means without, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: the quipu was the Inca memory device of knotted cords
U means upper-class and so socially acceptable

explanation.surface: Someone cracks a memory aid that is socially unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were Nancy Mitford's labels for upper-class and not, so U is socially acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisecrack is a witty remark, and 'crack' alone is short for it.

clue.text: Get killed moving about in the work cited by Tacitus

definitions.text: in the work cited by Tacitus
definitions.note: 'by Tacitus' flags that the phrase is Latin

indicators.note: letters moving about change places with one another

blocks.note: to cop it is British slang for being killed

explanation.surface: A Roman historian describes someone being killed in a mobile skirmish.
explanation.walkthrough: Tacitus was a Roman historian, so the phrase must be Latin. To cop it is British slang for being hurt or killed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin abbreviation of opere citato, used in footnotes to refer back to a work already cited.

clue.text: Supplier of light repast departs

blocks.note: tea is a light meal
the abbreviation in timetables

explanation.surface: A caterer serving snacks leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplier of light repast' reads as a caterer; 'light' belongs to the definition. Tead is Spenser's word for a torch.
explanation.definitionFit: A torch gives light; Spenser's archaic term for one is recorded in Chambers.

clue.text: A capsule in a refreshing form of healing

indicators.note: to refresh is to make new, and a new form means the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A pill in a refreshing form of medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is part of the fodder, not a container signal. Aesculapius was the Roman god of medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesculapius was the Roman god of medicine, so the adjective means relating to medicine or the healing art.

clue.text: Apostasy is being up to no good losing one in gathering

indicators.note: losing something leaves you without it, so a letter goes
one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a ring is a group of people gathered together
people 'at it' are up to mischief
the Roman numeral, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Abandoning the faith means misbehaving and losing someone at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: AT IT loses its I and sits inside the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat is to desert one's party or cause, so this gerund names defection or abandoning a faith.

clue.text: Excuse sensuality — certainly going free

indicators.note: something going free gets away, so those letters leave

blocks.note: sensual gratification
sure is an informal yes, certainly

explanation.surface: A defendant's excuse for indulgence, hoping to walk free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going free' sounds like acquittal, but it removes the letters for 'certainly'.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse offered to justify oneself, especially in court, is a plea, such as a plea of necessity.

clue.text: Zephaniah carries an amount of dry material

indicators.note: something carried is held inside, so the letters sit within the name

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively inside this prophet's name

explanation.surface: An Old Testament prophet carries a quantity of grain.
explanation.walkthrough: Zephaniah is an Old Testament prophet, which fits the Hebrew measure perfectly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrew unit of dry measure, also spelt ephah, used for grain, appears in the Bible.

clue.text: In short, ceps mostly dried quickly

definitions.note: the adverbial phrase stands for the past tense of the verb meaning to summarise, put in short

indicators.note: mostly means not entirely, so the last letter goes
something done quickly is hurried and jumbled, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written; ceps are porcini mushrooms
the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: Briefly put, the mushrooms were mostly dried in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' looks like the start of a summary sentence; it is the definition. Ceps are wild mushrooms.
explanation.definitionFit: To precis is to summarise, so a text reduced to a summary has been put in brief form.
